newsitem.title: INDIA: India to seek Italian's arrest in gun deal case.
newsitem.headline: India to seek Italian's arrest in gun deal case.

text.p: Indian police said on Saturday that two investigators had reached Malaysia to seek the arrest of a former employee of Italian firm Snamprogetti Spa linked by them to alleged payments by Sweden's Bofors AB in a gun deal.

Snamprogetti, an engineering firm, and the former employee, Ottavio Quattrocchi, on Friday denied any involvement in alleged payments by the arms maker, part of the Celsius group, connected with the $1.3 billion artillery contract in 1986.

S.M. Khan, spokesman of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), told Reuters by telephone that Revanna Siddaiah and N.R. Wasan were in Kuala Lumpur with a warrant to arrest and question Quattrocchi, who formerly represented Snamprogetti in India.
Khan said the CBI officials would seek the help of Malaysian authorities to arrest Quattrocchi.
"Yes," he said in response to a question on whether the CBI had a warrant to seek the Italian's arrest. "That (arrest) depends on the Malaysian authorities, but we will seek the arrest."

On Tuesday, Indian investigators released the names of five people they said had received money in connection with the contract that governed the 1986 sale of Bofors field guns to the Indian government.
Quattrocchi, who was the company's India representative when the contract was signed, and his wife, Maria, were among the five individuals named.
The CBI said documents obtained from Swiss authorities showed that the five had received payments from Bofors.
Swiss police have said there was evidence Bofors paid about $40 million into various banks accounts in Switzerland during the time the contract with India was drawn up and settled.
Quattrocchi, who lives in Malaysia, released a statement in Kuala Lumpur on Friday denying any involvement with the case.

"I wish to state emphatically and unequivocally that no relationship whatsoever has ever existed at any point in time between me and Bofors and consequently between me, Bofors and India or any Indian nationals," Quattrocchi said.
The furore over the alleged payments contributed to the defeat in 1989 of the government of late prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, who was accused of involvement in the affair.
Gandhi, who denied the allegations, was assassinated while campaigning for 1991 parliamentary polls.
On Friday, the Press Trust of India (PTI) quoted Quattrocchi as saying in a telephone interview that allegations surrounding the gun deal were aimed at damaging Gandhi's image.
"I have been a friend of Rajiv Gandhi and India. It has been a great honour for me to have known Rajiv Gandhi," the Indian news agency quoted him as saying.

The news agency said that Quattrocchi, asked why the CBI had named him in the case, said: "It is a political campaign being carried out for the last 10 years in India. They want to damage the image of a dead man."
Asked to comment on the PTI report in Kuala Lumpur, Quattrocchi told Reuters by telephone on Saturday: "I have not spoken and I will not speak to anybody."

In a front-page advertisement in the Times of India newspaper on Friday, Snamprogetti denied involvement and said that "recent press reports concerning the 'Bofors case' could damage the company's image".
"Snamprogetti has nothing to do with the matter under investigation," the Italian firm said in the advertisement.
"The present company representative in India appointed in January 1994, in accordance with Snamprogetti's policy, has already cooperated with CBI," it said.
A Snamprogetti executive in New Delhi confirmed that the firm had placed the advertisement.
Bofors said on Wednesday that it saw no need to reopen the investigation into the contract.
A Bofors spokeswoman in Stockholm said the firm had paid money as final payments to its agents, not as bribes.
